text.p: Sterling maintained its firm tone against the mark in Europe but was still shy of a fresh 52-month high seen in earlier trade.

Dollar/mark's rise to a 30-month high above 1.60 was the main driving force for sterling/mark's gains, traders said. But the stronger dollar also kept a lid on cable, slightly softer from late Thursday European levels.

"Sterling has been fairly quiet with trade dominated mainly by short-term speculative players," a dealer at a UK bank said. "We still expect sterling/mark higher but right now it's really dependent on what dollar/mark can do."
The pound shrugged off a larger than expected rise in the UK December public sector borrowing requirement.
The PSBR stood at 2.1 billion sterling against an average forecast of 1.1 billion. The cumulative April-December PSBR is now at 16.136 billion from 23.028 billion this time last year.
"The PSBR was disappointingly large but it does not make the government's full-year forecast look out of reach," said Jeremy Hawkins, economic adviser at Bank of America in London.
The UK Treasury said the PSBR figure was consistent with budget forecasts with borrowing in December boosted by shifts in the timing of interest rate payments.
By 1059 GMT, the pound was trading at 2.6813/20 marks, down from its early peak of 2.6865 marks but still above late Thursday's level of 2.6740/50.
Against the dollar, it was steady at $1.6725/35, slightly below $1.6759/69 on Thursday.
Chartists remained bullish on sterling's prospects against the mark, finding little resistance until the 2.70 mark level and above.
"The next real level is a double-bottom base above 2.70 marks seen in late 1989/early 1990 where it got down to around 2.7035," said Andrew Chaveriat, analyst at Banque Paribas in London.
Sterling held above this level until it crashed in September 1992, leaving a massive gap still waiting to be filled, technical analysts said.

The sudden death of a Conservative member of parliament pushed the ruling Conservative party into a minority, prompting speculation that a UK general election may be brought forward as early as March. The election must be held by May 22.
However, dealers said this prospect of an early vote had so far had a negligible impact on the pound with the sterling market choosing to take its next cues from the dollar.
